newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Surprise Australian rate catches markets off guard.
newsitem.headline: Surprise Australian rate catches markets off guard.

text.p: Australian financial markets were caught off guard on Wednesday when the central bank cut interest rates by half a percentage point to six percent, a move that stripped more than one U.S. cent off the Australian dollar.
The cut in the official cash rate by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) was the third in the past five months, following reductions on July 31 and November 6.
"This reduction essentially reflects a further improvement in the inflationary outlook," RBA Governor Ian Macfarlane said.

Macfarlane said the bank now expected inflation to stay below 2.5 percent for the remainder of 1996/97, citing the strength in the Australian dollar and recent national accounts data that suggested actual inflation could fall further.
But Macfarlane warned that rates would rise if Australia experienced a wage squeeze to control inflation -- a strategy the bank used three times in 1994.

While markets agreed with the cut, the timing took dealers by surprise, prompting the local dollar to be sold down sharply. From an early high of US$0.8020 on Wednesday, the Australian dollar fell to US$0.7900, where it stabilised.
"You've got to think the offshore guys will give it a belt," said one trader. "They're all focusing on yield differentials and the Australian dollars are getting perilously thin."
Lower Australian rates narrow the yield differential Australian assets enjoy over foreign assets, lessening their attractiveness to investors.
In contrast, bonds rallied on the rate cut. The benchmark 10-year bond yield initially dropped 30 basis points to around 7.08 percent, but came back to around 7.19 percent.

The rate cut kicked the Australian sharemarket higher at the opening, adding 21.2 points to the All Ordinaries index to 2,383, but concern that the economy may be weaker than many thought saw the gains pared by the afternoon session.
Markets had lowered their guard after no rate announcement was made last Wednesday, the day after the RBA board meeting, believing the next move would be held over until February.
"The timing is certainly a surprise, the direction and the magnitude are not," National Australia Bank economist Tim Pfitzner said. "We'd expected that maybe they'd wait for next year," he said.
It was a sentiment shared by others in the market.

Bankers Trust Australia chief economist Chris Caton said: "We were expecting this in early February after the next round of inflation data. The growth outlook for the economy is quite weak and inflation news is good, so this is the right decision."
However, not all agreed with the RBA's thinking in cutting rates again, especially just one month after the last cut.

"There may be an element of panic in this cut," said John Kyriakopoulos, senior economist with Macquarie Bank. "They must be more concerned about the economy than we thought, and particularly employment."
Official data last week saw the economy slowing to an annual growth of 3.8 percent from above five percent earlier in the year. The unemployment rate has stalled at about 8.5 percent.
But the RBA said the latest rate cut, founded on a strong Australian dollar, should boost economic growth and jobs.

On the trade weighted index (TWI), which measures the local unit against a weighted basket of currencies, the Australian dollar had risen more than 10 percent since the end of 1995, and more than 23 percent since its most recent trough in July 1995.
The official interest rate cut prompted two of Australia's major four banks, Commonwealth and Westpac, to cut their prime business lending rates by 0.5 percent to 9.25 percent.
"Overall, it is the bank's assessment that the economy has the capacity to grow a little faster without putting pressure on inflation," Macfarlane said.
"Today's easing, together with the two earlier ones, should provide an environment for stronger employment growth, subject to appropriate wage restraint," he said.
